title: Detecting and Remediating Drift
description: Find resources that were changed by hand in the portal and decide whether to import or revert them.

data.text: During an incident an engineer scaled up the App Service plan from P1v3 to P2v3 in the portal to survive a traffic spike. Two weeks later, a routine `terraform apply` from the pipeline plans to scale it back down. Nobody knows which value is correct. How should the team detect and handle this?

Treat hand-made changes as **drift that must be reconciled in code**. Run a scheduled `plan`/`what-if` in CI that fails (or opens a ticket) when it is not empty, so drift is visible within a day instead of at the next deployment. Then decide explicitly: either update the IaC to codify the emergency change (scaling up was right), or reapply the original code to revert it. In the portal, use **Azure Resource Graph** to spot resources whose tags or configuration no longer match the standard.

data.title: Scheduled drift detection in a pipeline
data.code:
schedules:
  - cron: '0 6 * * *'      # every morning
    displayName: Nightly drift check
    branches: { include: [ main ] }

steps:
  - script: terraform init -input=false
    displayName: Init
  - script: |
      terraform plan -input=false -detailed-exitcode -out=tfplan
      case $? in
        0) echo "No drift" ;;                    # 0 = no changes
        2) echo "##vso[task.logissue type=warning]Drift detected";
           terraform show -no-color tfplan;
           exit 1 ;;                             # 2 = changes pending
        *) exit 1 ;;                             # 1 = error
      esac
    displayName: Plan and fail on drift

data.title: Azure Resource Graph — find App Services without the required tag
data.code:
resources
| where type == 'microsoft.web/sites'
| extend owner = tostring(tags['owner']), env = tostring(tags['environment'])
| where isempty(owner) or isempty(env)
| project name, resourceGroup, location, owner, env
| order by resourceGroup asc

data.text: For a legitimate emergency change, codify it in the same sprint: bump the SKU parameter's allowed list and default, merge, and let the next apply be a no-op. Microsoft's `what-if` for Bicep and `terraform plan` for Terraform are the two preview mechanisms that make this safe.

Preventing all portal writes is tempting but brittle: during a real incident, an on-call engineer needs to act. Making drift **detectable and cheap to reconcile** keeps the emergency path open while ensuring the declared state in git remains the source of truth within a day.

cards.title: Deny portal writes via Azure Policy
cards.description: Lock resources to the IaC pipeline
cons: Policy scope mistakes lock out the platform team

cards.title: Ignore drift, converge on deploy
cons: Nobody learns what changed or why
